column1: # Curator sign-off. ONE LINE PER SIGNED RECORD. Nothing is signed today.
#   A named human read the record named in column 1, checked its sequence
#   against the accession its provenance cites, and wrote or checked its
#   description from the primary source. That is ReviewStatus::Reviewed's own
# WHAT content_sha256 IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
#   It is the digest of the row's semantic content -- Db::content_digest over
#   SIGNED_COLUMNS plus the record's provenance -- taken when it was signed. Its
#   job is STALE-APPROVAL DETECTION: if the sequence, the description, the
#   notes, the cited accession or the licence change afterwards, the digest
#   stops matching and the approval lapses automatically.
#   It is NOT authentication. The build computes the same digest from the same
#   content, so nothing about the hash stops a machine writing a valid-looking
#   line. Three things do, in descending strength:
#     1. The build never writes this file. It only reads it, and CI proves that
#        by running the build and requiring `git diff --exit-code` here.
#     2. build.py's coerce_row() refuses any stage that emits a review_status or
#        a curator, so a signature cannot be smuggled in from the other side.
#     3. Attribution is the git commit. Without code-signing certificates the
#        strongest claim available is "a human committed this line and git says
#        who". A detached signature (SIGNOFF.tsv.asc) can be added later and CI
#        will verify it when present; today the assertion rests on the commit
#        history and not on cryptography, and saying otherwise would be the same
#        species of overclaim this project exists to avoid.
#   A missing, blank, malformed, stale or unreadable sign-off can only ever
#   REMOVE trust, never add it. Every failure path resolves to 'proposed'.
#   1. Read the row. Actually read it, and there is a command for that:
#      It prints every column the signature covers, unescaped, plus the record's
#      provenance quads and the resulting digest -- i.e. the hash's own input,
#      rendered. Signing a digest nobody has read is not an attestation.
#   2. Take the 64 hex characters from that output, or run --print-digests for
#   3. Add one line below: the record id, 'reviewed' or 'verified', your name,
#      today's date, that 64-character digest, and a note saying what you
#   4. Rebuild. `check_signoff.py` and the Rust loader both recompute the digest
#      and will refuse it if it does not match.
#   --show and --print-digests WRITE NOTHING. They used to: both ran the whole
#   build and then its writer, and --out defaults to the source tree, so
#   "print me the digests so I can sign" silently republished features.tsv and
#   provenance.tsv underneath the curator. Both now return before the writer.
#   Replace the line; do not accumulate. Git already holds the history, and a
#   file that grows a line per re-signature stops being reviewable, which is the
#   only reason it is a TSV.
# ORDER OF WORK, learned the hard way and worth stating: change prose FIRST,
# then sign. `description` and `notes` are inside the digest, so rewriting them
# after signing lapses the signature and someone will be tempted to "fix" that
